title: How C++ Works
summary: You write **text** (source code). A **compiler** translates it into **machine code**. A **linker** joins the pieces into one **program** that your computer runs directly.
markdown:
## The big picture A computer's processor (the CPU) understands only numbers. Nobody wants to write programs as long lists of numbers, so we write them in a language people can read, and a tool translates that into the numbers the processor needs. C++ is one of those languages. The translating happens **before** the program runs. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["main.cpp
(what you write)"] --> C["Compiler
translates it"] C --> O["main.obj
(translated piece)"] O --> L["Linker
joins the pieces"] LIB["Standard library
(ready-made code)"] --> L L --> E["program.exe"] E --> R["The CPU runs it"] ``` | Step | What it does | Think of it as | |---|---|---| | **You write** | Type instructions into a text file ending in `.cpp` | Writing a recipe | | **Compiler** | Checks the file follows the rules of C++ and translates it | Translating the recipe into the cook's language | | **Linker** | Joins your translated code with ready-made library code | Binding the chapters into one book | | **Run** | The finished program starts | Cooking | You will hear three words constantly. They are worth learning now: - **Source code**: the text you write. - **Build** (or *compile*): turn source code into a program. This is both steps above, compiler then linker. - **Run**: start the program that was built. ## Why translate ahead of time? Some languages, such as Python, are translated a line at a time **while** the program runs. C++ does all of that work once, in advance. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph CPP["C++"] direction LR a1["Source code"] -->|"translated once"| a2["Machine code"] -->|"runs at full speed"| a3["CPU"] end subgraph PY["Python"] direction LR b1["Source code"] -->|"translated on every run"| b2["Interpreter"] --> b3["CPU"] end ``` > [!info] The trade > **You get speed.** Nothing stands between your program and the processor. That is why games, web browsers, operating systems and trading systems are written in C++. > **You pay with strictness.** The compiler refuses to build anything it cannot make sense of. That feels harsh in week one. Later you will be glad of it, because every mistake it catches is one that never reaches your running program. ## Three kinds of mistakes Every programmer makes all three, every day. Knowing which kind you are looking at tells you where to look. | When it shows up | Name | Example | Who notices | |---|---|---|---| | While building | **Compile error** | You forgot a `;` | The compiler. Nothing is built. | | While building | **Linker error** | You promised a function existed but never wrote it | The linker. Nothing is built. | | While running | **Logic error** (a *bug*) | It builds and runs, but prints the wrong total | Only you | > [!tip] Errors are not a judgement > A compile error is the compiler saying "I got stuck here". It gives you the line number. Read it, fix it, build again. Professionals do this hundreds of times a day. ## Where C++ came from ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1972
C"] --> B["1985
C++"] --> C["1998
first standard"] --> D["2011
modern C++"] --> E["2020
C++20"] --> F["2023
C++23"] ``` C++ gets a new version every three years, named after the year. This course teaches modern C++ (C++20, with the useful parts of C++23). You do not need to know the history yet; the full story is in [[13.10 C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next]]. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the job of the compiler? - It runs your program one line at a time as you type it - It finds the logic mistakes in what your program does + It checks your source code follows the rules of C++ and translates it into machine code - It stores your source code so the computer can read it later > The compiler checks the rules and translates source code into machine code; it cannot tell whether your program does what you meant. ? Your code builds fine but prints 5 when it should print 6. What kind of mistake is that? + A logic error - A compile error - A syntax error - A linker error > The build succeeded, so the code is valid C++. The compiler cannot know what you *meant*, so a wrong result is a **logic error**. ? What is the difference between building and running? - Building runs the program once to test it; running runs it for real - They are two names for the same step - Running turns source code into a program; building starts it + Building turns your source code into a program; running starts that program > **Building** produces the program from your source code and **running** starts it. If the build fails, there is nothing to run. ```

cards.q: What is the job of the compiler?
cards.a:
It checks your source code follows the rules of C++ and translates it into machine code

The compiler checks the rules and translates source code into machine code; it cannot tell whether your program does what you meant.

cards.q: Your code builds fine but prints 5 when it should print 6. What kind of mistake is that?
cards.a:
A logic error

The build succeeded, so the code is valid C++. The compiler cannot know what you *meant*, so a wrong result is a **logic error**.

cards.q: What is the difference between building and running?
cards.a:
Building turns your source code into a program; running starts that program

**Building** produces the program from your source code and **running** starts it. If the build fails, there is nothing to run.
